Jamal was halfway through a chess game with Hiroshi at the kitchen table in Leicester when his phone rang. A man's voice, fast and official: “This is your bank's security team. Your father's account gets frozen in ten minutes. A security code has just come to your phone. Read it to me now.”
Jamal's heart hammered. Dad was at work; a frozen account meant rent, the shopping, everything. His thumb was already opening his messages.
Then he stopped. Why ten minutes? he thought. Why is he so loud? Why do I feel like I can't breathe? A real bank would call Dad, not me. The hurry isn't a reason. The hurry is the trick.
“I'm not sharing any code,” he said, and hung up.
Hiroshi stared. “Was that real?”
“If it was real, it'll still be real in an hour,” Jamal said, and texted his dad.

qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.a: He was frightened and panicky, heart hammering, picturing his father's account frozen.

qa.a: Tell his dad and let him call the bank on the number printed on his card, never a number the caller gives.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi see what happened at the table?

The hostel common room was loud with a carrom match when Uday's phone buzzed with an unknown number. He stepped into the corridor.
“Sir, this is your father's bank. His account is being blocked in ten minutes due to verification failure. You will get an OTP. Just read it out and I will stop the block.”
Uday said nothing for a second, and the voice went sharper. “Nine minutes, sir. Hurry.”
He walked back into the room and said, loud enough for Elizabeth at the notice board to hear, “Why would a bank need me, in a hurry? Why is he counting down? When someone makes me panic like this, that's the part I should trust least.”
He cut the call. Elizabeth, the house prefect, came over. “Report it to the warden?”
“Yes. And I'm calling Papa now.”
Ten minutes later, Papa confirmed his account was fine.

qa.a: It suggests he felt a jolt of panic but steadied himself by naming the countdown out loud, turning the fear into a warning sign.

They took out the card and turned it over. Amma dialled the helpline printed on the back, not the one in the text. I heard Amma say, “No block? Nothing?” She was quiet for a bit after that, then hugged Chandrika with onion hands.
I don't know if Chandrika was scared. She looked very calm. Maybe too calm.

Dear Gopika Didi,
I owe you the real story, not just the sorry I said on the phone.
On Friday I got a message that looked like it came from the photo app, saying my account would be locked. I typed my password into the page it opened. The moment I pressed enter, I knew: the page had a strange web address. I felt so embarrassed that I told no one. I kept thinking I'd fix it myself somehow, and then I didn't.
On Sunday someone using my account messaged you pretending to be me, asking for a code “to recover my account”. You trusted me, so you sent it, and they got into yours.
If I had told Papa on Friday, he would have helped me change the password that night, and you'd never have got that message. Two days of hiding did this, not the click.
I've told Papa now. We changed everything and reported the account together.
Nitin

Computer teacher's note, Thursday, after period six
During the free period Wasim came to my desk white-faced. He had entered his login for the school learning portal on a page that came from a message, then noticed the web address was wrong. What struck me is what he had already done before reaching me. In the eight minutes since, he had changed the password on the real site, used the “log out of all devices” button, and switched on two-step verification with his phone. He showed me each screen.
He also asked whether the same password was used anywhere else. It was: his email. We changed that together. Then he phoned his father from my desk, because that email receives the family's bank alerts, and his father called the bank on the number from his card while we waited.
Afterwards Vinita, at the next computer, asked him how to switch on two-step verification.

Today's session used the booklet of common fraud examples. Most students read quietly. Mehak asked if she and Hafsa could act them out instead, and I agreed.
Hafsa played a “police officer” on a pretend call: “Your parcel had illegal items. Pay a fine or be arrested today.” Mehak's first answer was nervous: “But I didn't send anything...” She stopped and said to me, “If I argue, I'm already in the conversation. I need a line I can say without thinking.” She tried again: “I don't discuss this on calls. I'll go to the police station with my parents.” Then she put down the pretend phone.
They switched to a fake job offer asking for a registration fee. By the fourth try her refusal was steady and short.
Next week I will ask Mehak to lead a round with the Class Eight group.

Rehearsing felt silly back then. Francis kept doing a terrible accent. But it worked, and I didn't have to think at all.

Dear Dadi and Dada,
I'm leaving this letter with the card I've stuck next to your landline, so you know why it's there.
Last month your neighbour lost money to a caller who said he was from the bank. It scared me. So Divyansh and I wrote three rules in Hindi, in big letters:
1. OTP kabhi kisi ko mat batana. (Never tell anyone an OTP.)
2. Shak ho to phone rakho, aur ghar par phone karo. (If in doubt, hang up and ring someone in the family.)
3. Inaam ke liye paisa kabhi mat do. (Never pay money for a prize.)
Below the rules, Divyansh wrote Papa's number and mine.

passage:
So Vijay, you asked what I did in the holidays. Mostly this. I'm Omkar, and I became my grandparents' anti-scam teacher.
Nanaji had got two calls in one week: one “bank officer”, one “you've won a prize”. He didn't fall for them, but he told me he nearly pressed a button on the second. That scared me.
So I sat at their dining table with a sheet of chart paper and wrote in big Hindi letters: never share OTP; if unsure, hang up and call family; no payment for any prize. Nani made me add Mummy's number in red. We stuck it on the wall right above their landline, at eye level.
Then we practised. I'd ring the landline from my phone and play a fake officer, and Nani would read line two and hang up on me. She got very good at hanging up on me.
Last week a real one called. Nanaji just pointed at the chart and put the phone down.

qa.q: Where did they stick the chart paper?
qa.a: On the wall right above their landline, at eye level.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel on hearing that Nanaji nearly pressed a button?
qa.a: Omkar felt scared for Nanaji, and that worry pushed a practical plan into action.

qa.q: What made the plan work beyond the chart itself?
qa.a: The practice calls, because Nani rehearsed reading line two and hanging up until it felt natural.

qa.q: How did the plan look to Nanaji when the real call came?
qa.a: Nanaji felt sure enough to just point at the chart and put the phone down, with nothing left to decide.
